---
title: "Quiz: erosion and dilation"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. $A$ is the object (foreground) of a binary image, $B$ the structuring element (SE) with its origin; erosion $A \ominus B$ keeps the pixels where $B$ fits inside $A$, dilation $A \oplus B$ the pixels where the reflected $\check B$ hits $A$.

---

**Q1.** A mask has isolated noise pixels in the background. Which of erosion and dilation with a $3 \times 3$ square removes them, and what does it do to the real objects?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Can a $3 \times 3$ square fit inside a single pixel?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Erosion: the square does not fit inside an isolated pixel (or any object narrower than 3 pixels), so those disappear. But every real object also loses a one-pixel layer all round, and thin parts vanish. The next unit's **opening** (erode, then dilate) gives most of the size back.
:::

---

**Q2.** Dilate a single object pixel by an SE $B$. What is the result? And the erosion of a $1 \times 1$ object?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Dilation = a copy of $B$ placed on every object pixel.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The dilation is a copy of $B$ placed with its origin on that pixel. The erosion is empty unless $B$ is a single pixel: if $B = \{0\}$ the pixel survives; if $B = \{(1, 0)\}$ the result is the pixel one step to the left (where the SE, shifted right by one, lands on the object). With more than one SE pixel, nothing fits.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why does an SE that does not contain its origin behave strangely? Give an example.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Try $B = \{(1, 0)\}$, a single pixel one step to the right of the origin.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Then $A \ominus B = \{x : x + (1, 0) \in A\}$ is $A$ shifted one pixel to the **left**, and $A \oplus B$ is $A$ shifted to the right. Neither is contained in the other, so "erosion shrinks, dilation grows" no longer holds. The inclusions $A \ominus B \subseteq A \subseteq A \oplus B$ need $0 \in B$.
:::

---

**Q4.** Erosion with the min, dilation with the max over a window: why is erosion not a convolution, although it uses the same sliding window?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a convolution do with the sum of two images?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A convolution is linear: the result for $f + g$ is the sum of the results. The min is not: on a two-pixel window, $\min(0, 1) + \min(1, 0) = 0$ but $\min(0 + 1, 1 + 0) = 1$. Erosion is shift-invariant like a convolution, but not linear, so there is no impulse response that describes it and no frequency response.
:::

---

**Q5.** State the duality between erosion and dilation in words. Why does the SE get reflected?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
When is a pixel **not** in the erosion?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
"Eroding the object is dilating the background": $(A \ominus B)^c = A^c \oplus \check B$. A pixel is not in the erosion when $B$, placed there, has at least one pixel on the background, i.e. $B_x$ hits $A^c$. Dilation tests whether the **reflected** SE hits, so to write "$B_x$ hits $A^c$" as a dilation we must use $\check B$, whose reflection is $B$ again.
:::

---

**Q6.** You need to dilate a large image with a $21 \times 21$ square. How many max operations per pixel does the direct method need, and how many with the decomposition into a row and a column?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$A \oplus (B_1 \oplus B_2) = (A \oplus B_1) \oplus B_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Directly, 441 values per pixel (440 comparisons). The square is a row of 21 dilated by a column of 21, so two passes of 21 values each: 42 values (40 comparisons). With the van Herk / Gil–Werman running min/max, each line costs about 3 comparisons per pixel, whatever its length.
:::

---

**Q7.** The inner boundary $A \setminus (A \ominus B)$ is computed once with the cross and once with the $3 \times 3$ square. Which boundary is thicker, and which one is 4-connected?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which SE removes more pixels when eroding?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The square erodes more (a pixel must have all 8 neighbours in $A$ to survive), so its boundary contains more pixels: it is thicker and 4-connected (every boundary pixel touches the next by an edge). The cross only removes pixels with a 4-neighbour in the background; its boundary is thinner and 8-connected (it can step diagonally).
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that dilation distributes over union: $(A \cup C) \oplus B = (A \oplus B) \cup (C \oplus B)$. Does erosion distribute over union too?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Use $A \oplus B = \{a + b : a \in A, b \in B\}$. For erosion, try two objects that are each too small for $B$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$z \in (A \cup C) \oplus B \iff z = a + b$ with $a \in A \cup C$, $b \in B \iff z \in A \oplus B$ or $z \in C \oplus B$. Erosion does not: let $B$ be a row of 2 pixels, $A$ and $C$ two single pixels side by side. Each erosion is empty, but $A \cup C$ is a row of 2, whose erosion is one pixel. Erosion distributes over **intersection** instead: $(A \cap C) \ominus B = (A \ominus B) \cap (C \ominus B)$.
:::
